claim: Malaria transmission is spatially heterogeneous.
source: Malaria transmission is spatially heterogeneous.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the study's findings and cited literature.

claim: Spatial heterogeneity of malaria transmission reduces the efficacy of control strategies.
source: This reduces the efficacy of control strategies, but focusing control strategies on clusters or 'hotspots' of transmission may be highly effective.
evidence: This is stated as a known consequence of heterogeneity in the abstract.

claim: Focusing control strategies on clusters or 'hotspots' of transmission may be highly effective.
source: This reduces the efficacy of control strategies, but focusing control strategies on clusters or 'hotspots' of transmission may be highly effective.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction stated in the abstract.

claim: Among 1500 homesteads in coastal Kenya, the fraction of febrile children with positive malaria smears per homestead and the mean age of children with malaria per homestead were inversely correlated.
source: Among 1500 homesteads in coastal Kenya we calculated (a) the fraction of febrile children with positive malaria smears per homestead, and (b) the mean age of children with malaria per homestead. These two measures were inversely correlated, indicating that children in homesteads at higher transmission acquire immunity more rapidly.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study data.

claim: Children in homesteads at higher transmission acquire immunity more rapidly.
source: These two measures were inversely correlated, indicating that children in homesteads at higher transmission acquire immunity more rapidly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inverse correlation observed in the data.

claim: The inverse correlation between malaria positive fraction and mean age of children with malaria increased gradually with increasing spatial scale of analysis.
source: This inverse correlation increased gradually with increasing spatial scale of analysis, and hotspots of febrile malaria were identified at every scale.
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis of the data.

claim: Hotspots of febrile malaria were identified at every spatial scale.
source: This inverse correlation increased gradually with increasing spatial scale of analysis, and hotspots of febrile malaria were identified at every scale.
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis.

claim: Hotspots within hotspots were found down to the level of an individual homestead.
source: We found hotspots within hotspots, down to the level of an individual homestead.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the nested hotspot analysis.

claim: Febrile malaria hotspots were temporally unstable.
source: Febrile malaria hotspots were temporally unstable, but 4 km radius hotspots could be targeted for 1 month following 1 month periods of surveillance.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis of hotspots.

claim: 4 km radius hotspots could be targeted for 1 month following 1 month periods of surveillance.
source: Febrile malaria hotspots were temporally unstable, but 4 km radius hotspots could be targeted for 1 month following 1 month periods of surveillance.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the simulation analysis.

claim: Malaria transmission is determined by mosquito ecology and behavior.
source: Malaria transmission is determined by mosquito ecology and behavior, which is in turn determined by rainfall, hydrology, soils, human behavior and population distributions, and a range of other social, biotic and abiotic factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge in malaria epidemiology.

claim: Mosquito ecology and behavior is determined by rainfall, hydrology, soils, human behavior and population distributions, and a range of other social, biotic and abiotic factors.
source: Malaria transmission is determined by mosquito ecology and behavior, which is in turn determined by rainfall, hydrology, soils, human behavior and population distributions, and a range of other social, biotic and abiotic factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge in malaria epidemiology.

claim: Heterogeneity of malaria transmission is apparent at global scale.
source: Heterogeneity of malaria transmission is apparent at global scale (Gething et al., 2011), regional scale (Kleinschmidt et al., 2001a; Noor et al., 2009), and at fine scale in, for instance, Mali (Gaudart et al., 2006), Ghana (Kreuels et al., 2008), Ethiopia (Yeshiwondim et al., 2009) Kenya (Brooker et al., 2004; Ernst et al., 2006; Bejon et al., 2010), and Tanzania (Bousema et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Heterogeneity of malaria transmission is apparent at regional scale.
source: Heterogeneity of malaria transmission is apparent at global scale (Gething et al., 2011), regional scale (Kleinschmidt et al., 2001a; Noor et al., 2009), and at fine scale in, for instance, Mali (Gaudart et al., 2006), Ghana (Kreuels et al., 2008), Ethiopia (Yeshiwondim et al., 2009) Kenya (Brooker et al., 2004; Ernst et al., 2006; Bejon et al., 2010), and Tanzania (Bousema et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Heterogeneity of malaria transmission is apparent at fine scale in Mali, Ghana, Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania.
source: Heterogeneity of malaria transmission is apparent at global scale (Gething et al., 2011), regional scale (Kleinschmidt et al., 2001a; Noor et al., 2009), and at fine scale in, for instance, Mali (Gaudart et al., 2006), Ghana (Kreuels et al., 2008), Ethiopia (Yeshiwondim et al., 2009) Kenya (Brooker et al., 2004; Ernst et al., 2006; Bejon et al., 2010), and Tanzania (Bousema et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Spatial heterogeneity makes transmission relatively resilient to indiscriminate control efforts.
source: This spatial heterogeneity makes transmission relatively resilient to indiscriminate control efforts, but also provides an opportunity to engage in targeted malaria control on clusters of transmission (or 'hotspots'), a strategy that is predicted to be highly effective (Dye and Hasibeder 1986; Woolhouse et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a theoretical consequence supported by cited literature.

claim: Targeted malaria control on clusters of transmission (or 'hotspots') is predicted to be highly effective.
source: This spatial heterogeneity makes transmission relatively resilient to indiscriminate control efforts, but also provides an opportunity to engage in targeted malaria control on clusters of transmission (or 'hotspots'), a strategy that is predicted to be highly effective (Dye and Hasibeder 1986; Woolhouse et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a prediction supported by cited literature.

claim: Hotspots of malaria have been identified using active surveillance.
source: We have previously identified hotspots of malaria using active surveillance (Bejon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a previous study by the authors.

claim: Hotspots have been identified using passive surveillance in health facilities linked to demographic surveillance systems.
source: Others have identified hotspots using passive surveillance in health facilities linked to demographic surveillance systems (Ernst et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Passive surveillance is more readily scaled up than active surveillance.
source: Passive surveillance is more readily scaled up, but may be biased by variations in access to health care facilities and socially-determined health-seeking behavior (Sumba et al., 2008; Franckel and Lalou 2009).
evidence: This is a general statement about surveillance methods.

claim: Passive surveillance may be biased by variations in access to health care facilities and socially-determined health-seeking behavior.
source: Passive surveillance is more readily scaled up, but may be biased by variations in access to health care facilities and socially-determined health-seeking behavior (Sumba et al., 2008; Franckel and Lalou 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The incidence of febrile malaria presenting to health care is biased by access to care.
source: The incidence of febrile malaria presenting to health care is thus biased by access to care.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the previous statement.

claim: The malaria positive fraction (MPF) among children with fever controls for access to health care.
source: This bias may be countered by using the malaria positive fraction (MPF) among children with fever (also termed 'slide positivity rate' in some publications [Jensen et al., 2009]). The MPF includes all febrile children presenting to the dispensary as the denominator, hence controlling for access to health care, in contrast to incidence for which all children in the community are included in the denominator.
evidence: This is an explanation of the methodological approach.

claim: The MPF is less likely to show systematic spatial bias with distance from the health facility.
source: The MPF is less likely to show systematic spatial bias with distance from the health facility since parental accounts of illness have not been found to discriminate malaria from non-malarial fever (Luxemburger et al., 1998; Mwangi et al., 2005), and diagnostic testing is not available outside the dispensary.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and logical inference.

claim: Parental accounts of illness have not been found to discriminate malaria from non-malarial fever.
source: The MPF is less likely to show systematic spatial bias with distance from the health facility since parental accounts of illness have not been found to discriminate malaria from non-malarial fever (Luxemburger et al., 1998; Mwangi et al., 2005), and diagnostic testing is not available outside the dispensary.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Diagnostic testing is not available outside the dispensary.
source: The MPF is less likely to show systematic spatial bias with distance from the health facility since parental accounts of illness have not been found to discriminate malaria from non-malarial fever (Luxemburger et al., 1998; Mwangi et al., 2005), and diagnostic testing is not available outside the dispensary.
evidence: This is a statement about the local context.

claim: Data are collected from 1500 homesteads within an 8 km radius followed for 9 years.
source: Data are collected from 1500 homesteads within an 8 km radius followed for 9 years.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: Among approximately 20,000 febrile presentations from approximately 1500 different residences, 54% were positive for Plasmodium falciparum on blood smear examination.
source: Among ∼20,000 remaining febrile presentations from ∼1500 different residences, 54% were positive for Plasmodium falciparum on blood smear examination.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study data.

claim: The incidence of dispensary attendance declined with distance from the dispensary.
source: Using homestead as our unit of analysis, we found that the incidence of dispensary attendance declined with distance from the dispensary (on average −0.040 (95%CI 0.036–0.044) and −0.041 (95%CI 0.037–0.046) episodes per child year for each km for malaria smear positive and negative attendees, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: MPF was not found to vary significantly by distance of residence from the dispensary.
source: MPF was not found to vary significantly by distance of residence from the dispensary (from MPF = 0.50, 95%CI 0.47 to 0.54 at <2 km distance to MPF = 0.52, 95%CI 0.47 to 0.57 at 6–7 km, p=0.7).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Temporally stable spatial heterogeneity would be expected to lead to spatial heterogeneity in the acquisition of immunity.
source: Temporally stable spatial heterogeneity would be expected to lead to spatial heterogeneity in the acquisition of immunity, which may be evidenced by variation in the age profiles of children with febrile malaria.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation.

claim: Spatial heterogeneity in the acquisition of immunity may be evidenced by variation in the age profiles of children with febrile malaria.
source: Temporally stable spatial heterogeneity would be expected to lead to spatial heterogeneity in the acquisition of immunity, which may be evidenced by variation in the age profiles of children with febrile malaria.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation.

claim: MPF was inversely correlated with the average age of children with malaria (Spearman's rank correlation rs = −0.16, p<0.0001).
source: MPF was inversely correlated with the average age of children with malaria, Spearman's rank correlation (rs) = −0.16, p<0.0001 (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Greater exposure to malaria (i.e., high MPF) leads to more rapid acquisition of immunity as children grow up.
source: This suggests that greater exposure to malaria (i.e., high MPF) leads to more rapid acquisition of immunity as children grow up, hence predominantly younger children visiting the dispensary with febrile malaria.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inverse correlation.

claim: The average age of children with non-malarial fever did not show spatial clustering.
source: There was no evidence that this relationship was confounded by spatial clustering of age: the average age of children with non-malarial fever did not show spatial clustering (Moran's I = 0.01, p=0.5 within 1 km and Moran's I = 0.02, p=0.5 within 5 km) and was not associated with MPF (rs = −0.02, p=0.4).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The average age of children with non-malarial fever was not associated with MPF.
source: There was no evidence that this relationship was confounded by spatial clustering of age: the average age of children with non-malarial fever did not show spatial clustering (Moran's I = 0.01, p=0.5 within 1 km and Moran's I = 0.02, p=0.5 within 5 km) and was not associated with MPF (rs = −0.02, p=0.4).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The mean Spearman's rank correlation coefficient trended gradually away from 0 as the grid divisions became larger in scale.
source: We examined the effect of spatial scale at which this correlation occurred by imposing grids of increasing cell size on the study area, calculating rs within each cell of the grid, and then estimating the mean rs at each scale of grid (Figure 1D, blue lines). The mean rs trended gradually away from 0 as the grid divisions became larger in scale.
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The pattern of gradually increasing inverse correlation as grid size increases suggests gradual differentiation in transmission characteristics as the distance between homesteads increases.
source: This pattern suggests gradual differentiation in transmission characteristics as the distance between homesteads included within a cell of the grid increases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial analysis results.

claim: A hotspot with a radius of 5.8 km was identified at p<0.00001 using the full data set.
source: Using the Bernoulli model in SaTScan (Kulldorff, 1997), we identified a hotspot with a radius of 5.8 km at p<0.00001 (Figure 2A) using the full data set (for which n = 20,702).
evidence: This is a finding from the SaTScan analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A further hotspot with a radius of 0.76 km was identified within the 5.8 km hotspot (p<0.00001).
source: However, on re-analysis of the children within this hotspot (in which n = 5300), we identified a further hotspot (with a radius of 0.76 km) within the 5.8 km hotspot (p<0.00001, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the nested SaTScan analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A third significant hotspot (p=0.016) comprising a single homestead was identified within the 0.76 km hotspot.
source: Then on further re-analysis of the homesteads within that 0.76 km hotspot (within which n = 1406), we identified a third significant hotspot (p=0.016) which comprised a single homestead, in which there were 36 episodes of malaria compared with 3 malaria negative fevers (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the nested SaTScan analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In a single homestead hotspot, there were 36 episodes of malaria compared with 3 malaria negative fevers.
source: Then on further re-analysis of the homesteads within that 0.76 km hotspot (within which n = 1406), we identified a third significant hotspot (p=0.016) which comprised a single homestead, in which there were 36 episodes of malaria compared with 3 malaria negative fevers (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A hotspot with a 1.32 km radius (p<0.00001) was identified in a random 5-km square area outside the original 5.8 km radius hotspot.
source: When we selected a random 5-km square area outside the original 5.8 km radius hotspot, we identified a hotspot within this area a fourth hotspot with a 1.32 km radius (p<0.00001, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the SaTScan analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was an inverse correlation between the mean MPF and the variance in MPF over the 10-year study period (rs = −0.61, p<0.0001).
source: There was an inverse correlation between the mean MPF and the variance in MPF over the 10-year study period (rs = −0.61, p<0.0001, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Homesteads can be characterized as stable high transmission homesteads or unstable low transmission homesteads.
source: The temporal trends for two subsets of homestead can be seen in Figure 3B (stable high MPF) and Figure 3C (unstable low MPF), suggesting that homesteads can be characterized as stable high transmission homesteads or unstable low transmission homesteads.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal trends shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Infant parasite rates have been proposed as a measure of transmission intensity that minimizes the offsetting of acquired immunity in macro-epidemiological studies.
source: Infant parasite rates have been proposed as a measure of transmission intensity that minimizes the offsetting of acquired immunity in macro-epidemiological studies (Snow et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: MPF in children <1 year of age was strongly correlated with MPFs in children in the 1- to 2-year-old and 2- to 3-year-old age group.
source: In multivariable linear regression models, MPF<1yr was strongly correlated with MPFs in children in the 1- to 2-year-old and 2- to 3-year-old age group, but progressively less strongly correlated with MPF in older children (Figure 3Di).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis shown in Figure 3Di.

claim: MPF in children <1 year of age was progressively less strongly correlated with MPF in older children.
source: In multivariable linear regression models, MPF<1yr was strongly correlated with MPFs in children in the 1- to 2-year-old and 2- to 3-year-old age group, but progressively less strongly correlated with MPF in older children (Figure 3Di).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis shown in Figure 3Di.

claim: The variance in MPF<1yr was not correlated with MPFs in 1- to 2- or 2- to 3-year-old children.
source: On the other hand, the variance in MPF<1yr was not correlated with MPFs in 1- to 2- or 2- to 3-year-old children, but was progressively more strongly correlated with MPF in older children (Figure 3Dii).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis shown in Figure 3Dii.

claim: The variance in MPF<1yr was progressively more strongly correlated with MPF in older children.
source: On the other hand, the variance in MPF<1yr was not correlated with MPFs in 1- to 2- or 2- to 3-year-old children, but was progressively more strongly correlated with MPF in older children (Figure 3Dii).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis shown in Figure 3Dii.

claim: There were high stable transmission homesteads, with predominantly younger children getting febrile malaria, and low unstable transmission homesteads, with increasing risk to older children.
source: Hence there were high stable transmission homesteads, with predominantly younger children getting febrile malaria, and low unstable transmission homesteads, with increasing risk to older children.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the regression analysis results.

claim: The pattern of high stable vs low unstable transmission occurs between regions or countries.
source: This pattern of high stable vs low unstable transmission also occurs between regions or countries, and demonstrates a similarity between the micro- and macro-epidemiology of malaria (Hay et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: There is a similarity between the micro- and macro-epidemiology of malaria.
source: This pattern of high stable vs low unstable transmission also occurs between regions or countries, and demonstrates a similarity between the micro- and macro-epidemiology of malaria (Hay et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by cited literature.

claim: One week periods of surveillance did not identify hotspots that are still present the following week at fine spatial scales (less than 1 km).
source: One week periods of surveillance (top left panel of Figure 4) did not identify hotspots that are still present the following week at fine spatial scales (i.e., the plotted line indicates that the accuracy of targeting is 0% at scales of less than 1 km).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: At larger spatial scales, 1 week periods of surveillance resulted in the targeting of areas with a 60% excess of new malaria cases compared with the surrounding area at a scale of an 8 km diameter.
source: On the other hand, at larger spatial scales we found that 1 week periods of surveillance were more accurate, resulting in the targeting of areas with a 60% excess of new malaria cases compared with the surrounding area at a scale of an 8 km diameter.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis.

claim: Longer surveillance periods (e.g., 6 months) resulted in targeting areas with an excess of 20% malaria cases compared with the surrounding area over the range of spatial scales examined.
source: Longer surveillance periods (e.g., 6 months) resulted in targeting areas with an excess of 20% malaria cases compared with the surrounding area over the range of spatial scales examined.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis.

claim: Mass distributions of Insecticide Treated Nets (ITNs) in the area began in 2006.
source: Mass distributions of Insecticide Treated Nets (ITNs) in the area began in 2006.
evidence: This is a statement about the study context.

claim: Children using ITNs had a reduced risk of malaria (OR = 0.69, 95%CI 0.67 to 0.8, p<0.001).
source: We found that children using ITNs had a reduced risk of malaria by logistic regression (i.e., OR = 0.69, 95%CI 0.67 to 0.8, p<0.001), in keeping with previous literature on the personal protection provided by ITN use (Lim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from the logistic regression analysis.

claim: ITN use was not clustered spatially (Moran's I = 0.02, p=0.5).
source: On the other hand, we did not identify significant evidence that ITN use was clustered spatially (Moran's I = 0.02, p=0.5).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis.

claim: Adding ITN use as a covariate in SaTScan analysis to locate hotspots had little effect on results.
source: Furthermore, adding ITN use as a covariate in SaTScan analysis to locate hotspots had little effect on results; the addition of ITN use as a covariate changed the location of the hotspot by 120 m, and changed the predicted radius of the hotspot from 5.4 km to 5.2 km.
evidence: This is a finding from the SaTScan analysis.

claim: ITN use did not correlate with mean MPF<1yr (rs = −0.04, p=0.04).
source: We did not identify significant evidence that ITN use correlated mean MPF<1yr (rs = −0.04, p=0.04) or with the variance in MPF<1yr (rs = −0.01, p=0.7).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: ITN use did not correlate with the variance in MPF<1yr (rs = −0.01, p=0.7).
source: We did not identify significant evidence that ITN use correlated mean MPF<1yr (rs = −0.04, p=0.04) or with the variance in MPF<1yr (rs = −0.01, p=0.7).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: ITNs provided personal protection from malaria, but did not explain the spatial micro-epidemiological patterns.
source: Hence, ITNs provided personal protection from malaria, but we were unable to show that they explained the spatial micro-epidemiological patterns.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the ITN analysis results.

claim: Malaria cases were spatially heterogeneous in an 8-km radius area of coastal Kenya.
source: We found that malaria cases were spatially heterogeneous in an 8-km radius area of coastal Kenya.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: The strongly significant inverse correlation between the malaria positive fraction (MPF) and average age of children presenting with malaria suggests variable acquisition of immunity between homesteads.
source: The strongly significant inverse correlation between the malaria positive fraction (MPF) and average age of children presenting with malaria suggests variable acquisition of immunity between homesteads.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis.

claim: Homesteads at high transmission intensity have a high MPF and a young average age of malaria.
source: Homesteads at high transmission intensity have a high MPF and a young average age of malaria (with older children becoming immune and therefore not presenting to the dispensary) whereas homesteads at low transmission intensity have a low MPF but an older average age of malaria since older children are not becoming immune as rapidly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data patterns.

claim: Homesteads at low transmission intensity have a low MPF but an older average age of malaria since older children are not becoming immune as rapidly.
source: Homesteads at high transmission intensity have a high MPF and a young average age of malaria (with older children becoming immune and therefore not presenting to the dispensary) whereas homesteads at low transmission intensity have a low MPF but an older average age of malaria since older children are not becoming immune as rapidly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data patterns.

claim: The inverse correlation was present at every geographical scale examined within the study.
source: In fact there was no such discontinuity in the function shown in Figure 1D, indicating that the inverse correlation was present at every geographical scale examined within our study.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The pattern of spatial heterogeneity is relevant to malaria control, since targeted disease control is predicted to be highly effective.
source: The pattern of spatial heterogeneity is relevant to malaria control, since targeted disease control is predicted to be highly effective (Woolhouse et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Spatial targeting is particularly appropriate for malaria 'hotspots'.
source: Spatial targeting is particularly appropriate for malaria 'hotspots' (Coleman et al., 2009; Moonen et al., 2010; Bousema et al., 2012; Sturrock et al., 2013) and many malaria control programmes are already engaged in spatially-targeted intervention (Zhou et al., 2010; Loha et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Many malaria control programmes are already engaged in spatially-targeted intervention.
source: Spatial targeting is particularly appropriate for malaria 'hotspots' (Coleman et al., 2009; Moonen et al., 2010; Bousema et al., 2012; Sturrock et al., 2013) and many malaria control programmes are already engaged in spatially-targeted intervention (Zhou et al., 2010; Loha et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Malaria control programs can expect to identify hotspots at many different geographical scales.
source: Our data showing clustering at varying spatial scales suggest that malaria control programs can expect to identify hotspots at many different geographical scales.
evidence: This is an inference from the study findings.

claim: Using data aggregated over 1 month of surveillance to define 4 to 8 km diameter hotspots would provide greatest accuracy.
source: We found that using data aggregated over 1 month of surveillance to define 4 to 8 km diameter hotspots would provide greatest accuracy, but this information is only relevant for 1 month before temporal instability necessitates further surveillance.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the simulation analysis.

claim: Hotspot information is only relevant for 1 month before temporal instability necessitates further surveillance.
source: We found that using data aggregated over 1 month of surveillance to define 4 to 8 km diameter hotspots would provide greatest accuracy, but this information is only relevant for 1 month before temporal instability necessitates further surveillance.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis.

claim: A 6 km diameter hotspot south east of the dispensary maintained a 30–60% increase in MPF compared with the surrounding area throughout the 9-year surveillance.
source: For instance, we identified a 6 km diameter hotspot south east of the dispensary that maintained a 30–60% increase in MPF compared with the surrounding area throughout the 9-year surveillance.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: 61% of the children with positive microscopy slides would have malaria as the proximate cause of their illness, with the other 39% having chronic asymptomatic parasitaemia with co-incident fever from another cause.
source: Previous studies estimating malaria attributable fractions in the locality suggest 61% of the children in our analysis would have malaria as the proximate cause of their illness, with the other 39% having chronic asymptomatic parasitaemia with co-incident fever from another cause (Olotu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Spatial heterogeneity is more temporally stable when analysed for asymptomatic parasitaemia rather than febrile malaria.
source: We have previously demonstrated that spatial heterogeneity is more temporally stable when analysed for asymptomatic parasitaemia rather than febrile malaria (Bejon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a previous study by the authors.

claim: Targeting hotspots of asymptomatic parasitaemia would require community surveys rather than dispensary monitoring.
source: Targeting hotspots of asymptomatic parasitaemia would require community surveys rather than dispensary monitoring, which may need to be done less frequently than monitoring of febrile malaria episodes.
evidence: This is a logical inference about surveillance methods.

claim: MPF is not a comprehensive indicator of transmission intensity.
source: Furthermore MPF is not a comprehensive indicator of transmission intensity.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Homesteads with consistently low average ages of febrile malaria are likely to be stable high transmission homesteads which amplify transmission in the areas surrounding them.
source: Homesteads with consistently low average ages of febrile malaria are likely to be stable high transmission homesteads (such as those in subset p of Figure 3A) which amplify transmission in the areas surrounding them.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data patterns shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Targeting stable high transmission homesteads to interrupt transmission may be highly effective.
source: Targeting such high transmission homesteads to interrupt transmission may be highly effective (Woolhouse et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a prediction supported by cited literature.

claim: The spatial heterogeneity of transmission is progressively more stable at more coarse spatial scales.
source: The stronger inverse correlation between MPF and average age of febrile malaria as spatial scale increases (Figure 1) suggests that the spatial heterogeneity of transmission is progressively more stable at more coarse spatial scales.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mosquito ecology may be determined by altitude, cultivation practices, streams and dams, wind direction and mosquito searching behaviour for hosts.
source: Mosquito ecology may be determined by obvious geographical features such as altitude (Reyburn et al., 2005), cultivation practices (Lindsay et al., 1991), streams and dams (Ghebreyesus et al., 1999), wind direction (Midega et al., 2012) and mosquito searching behaviour for hosts (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Ecological models based on geographical features have been developed using frequentist techniques, Bayesian approaches, and fuzzy logic.
source: Ecological models based on such features have been developed using frequentist techniques (Omumbo et al., 2005), Bayesian approaches (Craig et al., 2007), and fuzzy logic (Snow et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The same ecological factor may act inconsistently in different geographical areas.
source: However, the same ecological factor may act inconsistently in different geographical areas (Kleinschmidt et al., 2001b; Gemperli et al., 2006; Noor et al., 2008), and the effect of ecological factors is modified by fine-scale vector and host movement (Perkins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The effect of ecological factors is modified by fine-scale vector and host movement.
source: However, the same ecological factor may act inconsistently in different geographical areas (Kleinschmidt et al., 2001b; Gemperli et al., 2006; Noor et al., 2008), and the effect of ecological factors is modified by fine-scale vector and host movement (Perkins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The environmental factors determining malaria transmission operate at a range of spatial scales.
source: Our data suggests that the environmental factors determining malaria transmission operate at a range of spatial scales.
evidence: This is an inference from the study findings.

claim: Mosquito breeding site density could be equally influenced by proximity to a large geographical feature such as a river, or to a micro-geographical feature such as a cow hoof-print.
source: We might speculate that mosquito breeding site density could be equally influenced by proximity to a large geographical feature such as a river, or to a micro-geographical feature such as a cow hoof-print (Sattler et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculation supported by cited literature.

claim: Ecological models of malaria transmission will need to include data at a range of spatial scales in order to accurately predict malaria risk.
source: Hence ecological models of malaria transmission will need to include data at a range of spatial scales in order to accurately predict malaria risk.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Pingilikani Dispensary is 40 km to the North of Mombasa, in Kilifi Country, Coast Province, Kenya.
source: Pingilikani Dispensary is 40 km to the North of Mombasa, in Kilifi Country, Coast Province, Kenya.
evidence: This is a description of the study location.

claim: The population relies mainly on subsistence farming and experiences all year round malaria transmission.
source: The population relies mainly on subsistence farming and experiences all year round malaria transmission, with 'long' and 'short' rains each year causing two peaks in transmission.
evidence: This is a description of the study population and context.

claim: Long and short rains each year cause two peaks in malaria transmission.
source: The population relies mainly on subsistence farming and experiences all year round malaria transmission, with 'long' and 'short' rains each year causing two peaks in transmission.
evidence: This is a description of the local transmission pattern.

claim: Between 2003 and 2011, data were collected on all children (≤15 years of age) attending the dispensary.
source: Between 2003 and 2011, data were collected on all children (i.e., ≤15 years of age) attending the dispensary.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: Demographic surveillance is conducted for 240,000 people in a 900 square kilometre area in Kilifi County.
source: Demographic surveillance is conducted for the 240,000 people in a 900 square kilometre area in Kilifi County.
evidence: This describes the demographic surveillance system.

claim: Four-monthly enumeration rounds were conducted to identify births, deaths, and migration.
source: Four-monthly enumeration rounds were conducted to identify births, deaths, and migration (3).
evidence: This describes the surveillance methodology.

claim: Analysis was restricted to within an 8 km radius of the dispensary, which accounted for >96% of all visits to the dispensary.
source: We restrict analysis to within an 8 km radius of the dispensary, which accounted for >96% of all visits to the dispensary and excluded visits with specific symptoms such as skin infections or cutaneous abscesses, otitis media, and gastroenteritis (>4 episodes diarrhoea per day) that might have been the primary motivation for seeking health care rather than fever per se.
evidence: This describes the study inclusion criteria.

claim: Visits with specific symptoms such as skin infections or cutaneous abscesses, otitis media, and gastroenteritis were excluded.
source: We restrict analysis to within an 8 km radius of the dispensary, which accounted for >96% of all visits to the dispensary and excluded visits with specific symptoms such as skin infections or cutaneous abscesses, otitis media, and gastroenteritis (>4 episodes diarrhoea per day) that might have been the primary motivation for seeking health care rather than fever per se.
evidence: This describes the study exclusion criteria.

claim: The excluded visits combined accounted for 14% of all visits.
source: These latter exclusions combined accounted for 14% of all visits.
evidence: This is a finding from the data.

claim: All children presenting for assessment (except those with trauma as their only concern) had finger-prick blood samples examined for malaria parasites.
source: All children presenting for assessment (except those with trauma as their only concern) had finger-prick blood samples examined for malaria parasites.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic procedure.

claim: Thick and thin blood smears were stained with 10% Giemsa and examined at x1000 magnification for asexual Plasmodium falciparum parasites.
source: Thick and thin blood smears were stained with 10% Giemsa and examined at x1000 magnification for asexual Plasmodium falciparum parasites.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic procedure.

claim: 100 fields were examined before slides could be considered negative.
source: 100 fields were examined before slides could be considered negative.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic procedure.

claim: Amodiaquine was the first-line anti-malarial from 2003 to 2005.
source: Amodiaquine was the first-line anti-malarial from 2003 to 2005, when policy changed to Co-artemether.
evidence: This describes the treatment policy.

claim: Policy changed to Co-artemether in 2005.
source: Amodiaquine was the first-line anti-malarial from 2003 to 2005, when policy changed to Co-artemether.
evidence: This describes the treatment policy change.

claim: Fever was defined as either reported fever by the parents or measured fever (axilliary temperature ≥37.5°C).
source: Fever was defined as either reported fever by the parents or measured fever, that is, axilliary temperature ≥37.5°C (Mackowiak et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes the case definition.

claim: Multiple identifications of fever and parasitaemia in the same child within 21 days were considered a single episode.
source: Multiple identifications of fever and parasitaemia in the same child within 21 days were considered a single episode.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach.
